teaser.text: Illinois Tool Works is a global manufacturer of specialized industrial products and equipment. It earns money by selling those products and services for more than it costs to make, support, and deliver them.

paragraphs.text: The weighted path reaches $280.55 in October 2027, a 6% return including dividends. It reaches $284.48 in October 2028, a 10% return including dividends. By October 2029, it reaches $300.14, a 19% return including dividends.

blocks.heading: What could go right or wrong for ITW?

paragraphs.text: The bear case requires the 2026 acceleration to fade while customers defer equipment and construction spending remains weak. Tariffs or raw-material inflation could arrive before price recovery, and CBI could fail to replace simplified product lines. Cash conversion would remain below plan, so dividends and buybacks would pressure equity and debt would compress the multiple. The price falls from $175.44 in 2027 to $80.06 in 2029. Its 28% probability reflects the raised outlook's dependence on a second-half acceleration and the first-half cash shortfall.

The bull case requires repeat CBI purchases across segments, recovery beyond electronics and welding, timely pricing, and stronger cash conversion. The price rises from $399.89 in 2027 to $702.08 in 2029. Its 15% probability reflects a credible growth route that public disclosure has not yet proved durable.

blocks.heading: How much cash does ITW really make?

paragraphs.text: The memo’s “real” free cash flow subtracts stock compensation. Share-based pay does not require immediate cash, but it is still a cost to owners because it dilutes their claim. Second-quarter 2026 free-cash-flow conversion was 77%, which ITW described as seasonal; the full year matters more than one quarter.

Free cash flow is the cash left after operations and spending on new equipment and facilities. It differs from accounting profit because a sale may be recorded before the customer pays, while inventory may absorb cash before it is sold. In 2025, ITW reported $3.126 billion of operating cash flow. It spent $419 million on plant and equipment, leaving $2.707 billion of free cash flow.

dividend.closing: The full memo also answers how ITW makes money, compares with rivals, assesses management, and weighs its risks.

blocks.heading: How much does ITW pay its shareholders?

paragraphs.text: The 2026 policy continues the approach. The board authorized up to $6 billion of repurchases and raised the dividend by 7%. The quarterly dividend became $1.72. The central question is not whether ITW can distribute cash, but whether those distributions are covered by recurring cash after the business funds its future.

The dividend begins from the $6.88 annualized run rate after the latest $1.72 quarterly payment. The base case applies roughly 7% annual increases, reaching $8.43 per share in 2029, because dividends have risen from $4.72 in 2021 to $6.22 in 2025. The bear case holds the rate initially and then grows it by 2%, while the bull case applies 9% growth. The restraint reflects first-half free cash flow of $1.159 billion against $1.583 billion of net income.

blocks.heading: Is ITW's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: ITW’s shareholder payments exceeded its annual free cash flow in every year shown.

Free cash flow is the cash left after normal operations and spending on plant and equipment. It is the pool a company can use for dividends, buybacks, acquisitions, and debt repayment. If payouts exceed that pool, the company must use cash already held, sell assets, or borrow.

earnings.title: ITW earnings date
earnings.meta_description: ITW reports on October 27, 2026; management expects growth, margins, and cash conversion to arrive together.
earnings.opening: ITW is scheduled to report results on October 27, 2026. Watch whether growth broadens beyond capex-sensitive businesses.
earnings.closing: The full ITW memo also answers questions about its business, rivals, management, and risks.

paragraphs.text: Management’s raised 2026 outlook depends on growth and profitability arriving together. The July 28 forecast calls for GAAP earnings per share of $11.35–$11.55, with midpoint growth of 9% and implied second-half organic growth of 4.5%. GAAP earnings per share are profit per share under standard accounting rules; organic growth excludes acquisitions and currency effects.

Management also expects companywide initiatives to add at least one percentage point to operating margin. A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Simplifying products, improving purchasing, and reducing overhead can make more of each new sales dollar become operating profit; under ITW’s incremental-margin assumption, about 40 cents of an additional dollar would do so. ITW also expects free cash flow to exceed net income, so the next test is whether sales, margins, and cash conversion improve together.

blocks.heading: What has ITW's revenue and profit trend been over the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: The longer pattern is uneven. Revenue rose sharply earlier in the period, then contracted before edging higher again. The segment split matters because Automotive OEM, Welding, Food Equipment and Specialty Products grew organically in 2025, while Construction Products, Test & Measurement and Electronics, and Polymers & Fluids declined.

blocks.heading: What should people watch in ITW's next results?

paragraphs.text: The next major test is whether ITW’s second-half growth appears broadly and produces cash. ITW is scheduled to report third-quarter results on October 27, 2026. Investors should look beyond total sales to see whether demand spreads beyond capex-sensitive businesses, while checking whether margins and cash conversion hold.
The main takeaway is simple: ITW’s plan is financially possible, but only if growth broadens, margins remain strong, and operating cash catches up with shareholder commitments.
